content: We have docs#IsSupClosedCompact and docs#IsSupFiniteCompact, which are predicates on complete lattices. We also have the theorem docs#CompleteLattice.wellFoundedGT_characterisations, which tells us that both of them are equivalent to docs#WellFoundedGT. So... why do we have them?

I think it'd make more sense to restructure the file so that it proves the theorems

  • WellFoundedGT α ↔ [definition of IsSupClosedCompact α]
  • WellFoundedGT α ↔ [definition of IsSupFiniteCompact α]

And deprecate the predicates themselves.
@Snir Broshi who was working with this file recently
this looks similar to the situation in #mathlib4 > three dedekind domains
the solution I executed there is to make them private and modify the theorems at the end expressing the equivalence to unfold the duplicate
we also have docs#FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsSatisfiable and docs#FirstOrder.Language.Theory.IsFinitelySatisfiable in the same sort of situation

Thanks for the ping!
I agree that these are redundant ATM and with the iff solution, although that's only because they're restricted to CompleteLattice.

IMO we should add a class for "every element is compact" (equivalently, Set.Iic is Scott continuous) for preorders (perhaps called IsCompactOrder?).
e.g. consider ℕ: every element is compact, but > is not well-founded.

Compared to docs#IsCompactlyGenerated, I think this is similar to the difference between docs#TopologicalSpace.NoetherianSpace and docs#CompactlyGeneratedSpace, everything is compact vs compactly generated.
Topology has both notions, and order theory should have as well.
